parts.text:
Study Sources A and B.
How far does Source A support the evidence of Source B about the condition of Russian workers before 1914?
Explain your answer.

markscheme.general: This question tests AO3 (analysing and comparing sources). Comments on the reliability or provenance of the sources are not required and gain credit only where they are used to explain the extent of support.

grid.descriptor: A simple comparison based on surface details of the sources, with little support taken from them.
A developed comparison identifying agreement and/or difference, supported with detail from both sources. Maximum 4 marks unless both agreement and difference are considered.
An analytical comparison of agreement and difference, well supported from both sources, with a reasoned overall judgement on how far Source A supports Source B.

indicative: Agreement: both sources suggest that workers' living and working conditions were very poor. Source A: twelve people sleep in one room and workers are fined. Source B: the barracks are crowded and dirty and wages are low.
Agreement: both sources suggest that workers were angry and ready to protest. Source A: some men want to strike again. Source B: discontent is growing among younger workers.

Difference: Source A suggests that the government did more to control workers than to help them (the police keep lists of workers' names, so the authorities watch rather than help them); Source B does not support this point.
Overall, Source A gives strong support to Source B, although there are some differences of emphasis.
levels.credit_note: Indicative content is not exhaustive: credit any other valid points.

figures.label: Source A: From a letter written by a textile worker in St Petersburg to her brother in the countryside, 1907.
figures.text: We sleep twelve to a room in the barracks next to the mill, and the air is so thick you can hardly breathe. The foreman fines us for talking and for every broken thread. Some of the men say we should strike again as we did in 1905, but I am afraid. They say the police have lists of all our names.

figures.label: Source B: From a report by a factory inspector employed by the government, 1910.
figures.text: In the larger works of the capital there has been some improvement. Hours have been reduced in several factories, and a few owners have built schools and clinics. Nonetheless, the barracks remain crowded and dirty, and wages have not kept pace with the price of bread. I fear that discontent is growing among the younger men.

figures.text: Free Russia has the freest government in the world. We have abolished the death penalty, freed the prisoners and given equal rights to all peoples. Soon the Constituent Assembly will decide our future. Our soldiers will defend this freedom against the German Kaiser.

figures.label: Source B: From the memoirs of a British diplomat in Petrograd, published in 1923.
figures.text: The new government's decrees on freedom of the press and religion were admirable on paper, and Kerensky spoke beautifully, but he could not act. The June offensive collapsed, the army melted away and deserters filled the trains. The government's orders meant nothing beyond the capital. By the autumn it was obvious that whoever was bold enough could seize power.
figures.provenance: Original source written for this practice question. It is attributed to an invented, unnamed person of the period and is not a real historical document.

figures.label: Extract C: From a study of Kerensky, published in 2011.
figures.text: The Provisional Government was weak from the start. It had not been elected, it had no reliable army and it shared power with the Petrograd Soviet. indicative: Extract C argues that the October Revolution was a coup rather than a popular rising; it says that it was a carefully planned coup and most people were hardly aware that anything had happened.

Support from Source B: it suggests that the Bolsheviks had little popular support (it calls them a small group of conspirators acting behind the people's backs).
Own knowledge supporting the interpretation: Only a few thousand Red Guards, soldiers and sailors were involved.
Own knowledge supporting the interpretation: The Bolsheviks acted before the Congress of Soviets met.
Own knowledge supporting the interpretation: The Bolsheviks won only about a quarter of the votes in the Constituent Assembly elections.
Own knowledge challenging the interpretation: The Bolsheviks had won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets.
Own knowledge challenging the interpretation: The Congress of Soviets approved the new government.
Own knowledge challenging the interpretation: Bolshevik membership had grown to around a quarter of a million.
A Level 4 answer reaches a clear judgement on how far it agrees, weighing the evidence of the sources and own knowledge against the view in Extract C.

Own knowledge supporting the interpretation: Other socialist parties were later banned.
Own knowledge challenging the interpretation: Left Socialist Revolutionaries joined the government in December 1917.
Own knowledge challenging the interpretation: Lenin allowed the Constituent Assembly elections to go ahead.
Own knowledge challenging the interpretation: Power was formally held by the Congress of Soviets.
A Level 4 answer reaches a clear judgement on how far it agrees, weighing the evidence of the sources and own knowledge against the view in Extract C.

indicative: Agreement: both sources suggest that grain was taken from the peasants by force. Source A: the squads searched under the floorboards and in the stoves. Source B: grain is taken from the kulaks.
